mula_devanagari: इच्छा द्वेषः सुखं दुःखं संघातश् चेतना धृतिः | एतत् क्षेत्रं समासेन स-विकारम् उदाहृतम्
mula_iast: icchā dveṣaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ saṃghātaś cetanā dhṛtiḥ | etat kṣetraṃ samāsena sa-vikāram udāhṛtam
jayatirtha_prameyadipika: ।।13.7।।महाभूतानीत्यनुक्रम्यएतत्क्षेत्रं समासेन सविकारमुदाहृतं इत्युक्तम्? तत्र न ज्ञायते किं क्षेत्रं के च तद्विकारा इत्यत आह -- इच्छादय इति। पूर्वं क्षेत्रमिति भावः।

current_dvaita_rendering.english: Desire and the rest are the vikāra (modifications).
current_dvaita_rendering.divergence_note: THIN. Madhva (his 13.7) supplies a single sentence connecting 'desire and the rest' to 'sa-vikāram'. It does not say whether desire belongs to the self or the mind, nor how cetanā or dhṛti are taken. No further Dvaita reading can be drawn from the source.

current_dvaita_everyday: Madhva says only that desire and the rest are modifications, without saying whose. So the plain lesson is the verse itself: your wants and dislikes change, which makes them part of what you work with, not fixed facts about you. Anything more Dvaita-specific would be invented.

other_schools_english.advaita: Icchā (desire): having once met a kind of thing as a cause of pleasure, on meeting its like one wants to take it; this is a property of the inner organ and, because it is known (jñeyatvāt), it is field; so too dveṣa (aversion), sukha (pleasure), clear and serene, and duḥkha (pain), all field because all are known. Saṃghāta is the aggregate of body and senses; cetanā is the modification of the inner organ shown in it, shot through with the reflected light of the self's consciousness as an iron ball is with fire; dhṛti is what holds up body and senses when they sink; and these too are field because they are known. Desire and the rest stand for every property of the inner organ: this is the field with its modifications, from the great elements to dhṛti, stated in brief.
other_schools_english.viśiṣṭādvaita: Desire, aversion, pleasure and pain are called the field's products and modifications: although they are properties of the self (ātma-dharma), they arise from its connection with the field, and so are counted as the field's effects, the puruṣa being, as I shall say, the cause of experiencing pleasure and pain. Read 'cetanādhṛtiḥ' as one word: the saṃghāta (aggregate of elements) is the ādhṛti (support) of the cetana (conscious one), arisen as the base for the one who tastes pleasure and pain and who achieves both experience and release. This is the field, in brief, with its effects.
other_schools_english.śuddhādvaita: Now its modifications: though desire, aversion, pleasure and pain are properties of the self, they belong to it as my cit-aṃśa (spark of consciousness) only through its tie to the field, so they are said to rest in the field; and saṃghāta is the compact body, cetanā the life-functions such as breath that carry discernment, and dhṛti steadiness. This body made of elements was brought forth by my icchā (will) for devotion to me, a support for the puruṣa who is my spark and in truth unmanifest, so that tasting pleasure and pain he may win both experience and release; it is thick with desire and aversion, yet a means to all four aims of life, sealed by destiny and by others. This perishable field, the human body gross and subtle, I have set out for you in brief!
other_schools_english.bhakti: Desire and the rest are familiar; saṃghāta is the body, cetanā the mind's cognitive modification, dhṛti steadiness. Because they are seen (dṛśyatvāt), desire and the rest are not properties of the self but properties of the mind, and so fall inside the field; they stand also for intention and the like, as śruti says: 'desire, intention, doubt, faith, unfaith, steadiness, unsteadiness, shame, understanding, fear: all this is mind alone'. So the field's properties promised under 'what it is like' are shown, and this field with its modifications, the senses and the rest, I have told you in brief.
other_schools_english.advaita-bhakti: Icchā is the mind-state that craves pleasure and its means, called kāma or rāga; dveṣa its opposite, called krodha or envy; sukha a mind-state wanted for its own sake, born of dharma, which gives a glimpse of the bliss of the paramātman; duḥkha its opposite, born of adharma; saṃghāta the body with its senses; cetanā the mind-state, born of valid knowing, that reveals the self's own knowledge; dhṛti the effort that holds up flagging body and senses: all mind, as śruti says. Against the materialist who says the body-aggregate is the conscious knower, the Buddhist for whom momentary cognition is the self, and the logician for whom desire and the rest are marks of the self, the word 'sa-vikāram' answers: all of this undergoes change from birth to destruction, and a changing thing cannot witness its own arising and passing, so the witness of every change is itself changeless. As it is said, 'of a thousand changes in the intellect I am the witness, therefore changeless'; changeability, not counting, is the mark of the field.
